name: Functional movement disorder
aliases: functional neurological disorder with movement symptoms

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / functional neurological disorder literature
clinicalPearls: Abnormal movements such as tremor, dystonia, myoclonus, gait disturbance or parkinsonism that are internally inconsistent and incongruent with recognised neurological disease
It is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical signs, not merely the absence of another disorder
Functional tremor characteristically changes frequency and entrains to the rhythm of a voluntary movement in the other limb
Distractibility, variability, suggestibility and a sudden onset are supportive features
It sits within the broader category of functional neurological disorder and may coexist with genuine organic disease
Clear explanation of the diagnosis and multidisciplinary rehabilitation, including physiotherapy and psychological therapy, are central to management
reference.pathophysiology: Functional movement disorder is understood as a disorder of abnormal motor control and self-agency rather than structural damage, in which movements are generated through mechanisms overlapping with voluntary movement yet experienced as involuntary. Current models emphasise aberrant attention directed to the affected body part, abnormal predictive processing and altered sense of agency, often in the context of predisposing, precipitating and perpetuating psychological and physical factors. The internal inconsistency of the movements reflects their dependence on attention and expectation.
additionalDifferentials: Myoclonus of structural or metabolic cause
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical examination eliciting positive functional signs (entrainment, distractibility, variability)
Targeted investigation only to exclude specific mimics suggested by the history
Neurophysiology (for example tremor recording with entrainment testing) in selected cases
Assessment of comorbid mood, anxiety and other functional symptoms
Avoidance of excessive or repeated testing that can reinforce illness beliefs
redFlags: Features that are in fact typical of an organic disorder on review
Progressive fixed deficits or abnormal imaging
Coexisting organic disease requiring its own treatment
Significant psychiatric comorbidity or risk requiring urgent attention
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are variable but early diagnosis, a clear positive explanation and engagement with multidisciplinary therapy are associated with better recovery; long-standing untreated symptoms can be more refractory.
pitfalls: Treating it purely as a diagnosis of exclusion rather than demonstrating positive signs
Over-investigating and inadvertently reinforcing the disorder
Communicating the diagnosis poorly, which undermines engagement and recovery
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Give a clear, positive rule-in explanation of the diagnosis using the demonstrated signs such as entrainment and distractibility
Specialist functional-movement physiotherapy to retrain movement and normalise motor control
Psychological therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy for precipitating and perpetuating factors
Multidisciplinary rehabilitation with occupational therapy and speech therapy where needed
Treat comorbid mood, anxiety and pain
Avoid unnecessary investigations and ineffective medications that risk iatrogenic harm
Escalate to a specialist functional-disorder service for refractory or complex presentations
